Used commercial kitchen equipment has long traded through a broken pair of channels: auctioneers and local dealers who buy at steep discounts, or storage, where a closing restaurant's range line sits indefinitely. Buyers inherit a market with no condition standards and no delivery, while sellers field lowball calls for weeks. Forkfleet's framing of the gap is blunt — a six-burner range that listed for $4,000 new is worth real money only if a buyer can trust the burners fire, get it to their kitchen, and the seller avoids spending three weekends on the phone. Auctions, in the company's telling, solve none of that; classifieds solve less.

The product is a marketplace that inserts inspection and freight between the two sides. Sellers photograph equipment in the Forkfleet app and receive an estimate from comparable completed sales in their market; an inspector then verifies condition — burners, compressors, door seals, temperature calibration — before the listing goes live with a graded report. Buyers see that report, financing options, and a delivery quote. Forkfleet books freight through partner carriers with restaurant-equipment experience, including blanket wrap, liftgate delivery, inside placement where building access allows, and haul-away of old equipment on the same trip. Nothing is consigned to a warehouse: equipment stays with the seller and ships directly to the buyer.

The condition standard is the company's most specific piece of machinery. Lists are graded A, B, or C — A means inspected with no functional issues, B means cosmetic wear but fully functional, C means a disclosed functional issue priced accordingly. Listings show the inspector's individual checks: burner ignition, compressor amperage, door-seal integrity, temperature calibration against a reference probe. Inspectors work a written, public per-category protocol — every burner fired and the oven cycled to temperature on ranges; compressor draw measured and pull-down time logged on refrigeration; pump pressure and boiler checks on espresso machines — and photograph each checkpoint. Equipment that fails is either re-priced as Grade C with the defect disclosed or declined.

The pricing engine is built on completed Forkfleet sales rather than asking prices or depreciation curves: model, age, grade, market, and season. A Grade B convection oven in Chicago prices against what Grade B convection ovens actually sold for in Chicago over the last two quarters, and sellers see both the estimate range and the count of comparable sales behind it. Listing price remains the seller's choice, but the estimate is where offers converge, and hot categories — espresso equipment in spring — move with demand. A blog post on walk-in compressor values argues compressor hours matter more than age.

Users span closing restaurants, renovations, landlords recovering abandoned equipment, restaurant groups consolidating locations, and food trucks and ghost kitchens outfitting a kitchen. Closures and renovations remain the busiest use case and the origin story: one inspector visit can catalog an entire kitchen, including smallwares lots, and the seller approves the batch from the app. Licensed dealers also list under the same standard, with bulk listing tools and storefront pages; about a fifth of listings come from dealers, and the company's stated point is that buyers shouldn't have to care who the seller is.

On economics, Forkfleet charges sellers an 8 percent commission per sale and buyers a flat service fee shown before checkout, with financing through a lending partner and same-day approval decisions typically. There are no listing fees and no monthly fees. Every purchase carries a 48-hour acceptance window for running the equipment against the report, followed by a 30-day working guarantee that Forkfleet itself honors — repair, replacement, or refund — rather than the seller. The company publishes guarantee claims rates by category and grade; it says Grade B refrigeration, its highest-volume category, runs under 3 percent.

Founded in Chicago in 2019 by Nate Kowalski, a decade-long equipment dealer and auctioneer, and Maria Reyes, who built logistics software for a freight brokerage, Forkfleet has expanded to 12 metro markets — Chicago, Milwaukee, Minneapolis, Detroit, Indianapolis, Columbus, Cleveland, St. Louis, Kansas City, Nashville, Atlanta, and Dallas — and lists over 5,000 items at any time. Sellers can list only where inspectors are, but buyers purchase from anywhere in the continental US with freight quoted to the door. New markets open when inspector coverage is ready. The company is 45 people, with inspectors and market managers in each metro, logistics coordinators, and engineering behind the pricing engine and app, and it currently hires inspectors in Dallas and Atlanta, a Chicago freight coordinator, and a remote senior mobile engineer. Trade press coverage, per the site, has focused on the grading standard and the asset-light seller-to-buyer freight model that let a 45-person company operate across 12 markets.
